title: Terminal deletion of 5p
clinical_history: A 4-month-old infant is referred because of a high-pitched cry, microcephaly, hypertelorism, and developmental delay. High-resolution constitutional chromosome analysis is requested.
unknown_prompt: An infant with a high-pitched cry, microcephaly, and developmental delay is referred for constitutional cytogenetic analysis. Examine chromosome 5 carefully, then complete the karyotype, ISCN, and clinical correlation.
plain_language_interpretation: A female karyotype with 46 chromosomes and a terminal deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 with a breakpoint at band p15.2.
explanation: One chromosome 5 has a shortened p arm; the total count remains 46, so this is a structural rather than a numerical abnormality. ISCN writes a terminal deletion as del(5)(p15.2) after the sex-chromosome complement. The corresponding constitutional syndrome is cri-du-chat (5p deletion) syndrome. Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome is a 4p deletion and should not be selected from p-arm morphology of chromosome 5 alone. In this demonstration set the deleted homolog is drawn with a truncated p arm; authentic cases are confirmed by banding and often by FISH or microarray.
hints: The chromosome count is still 46, so look for a structural change rather than an extra or missing whole chromosome.
Compare the two chromosomes in pair 5. Group B chromosomes are large submetacentrics; a shortened p arm is the key finding.
Terminal deletions are written del(chromosome)(arm and band), for example del(5)(p15.2).
